observation_summary: The application throws an OutOfMemoryError when fitting a large number of points because it attempts to allocate an n x n full matrix for weights, even when the weight matrix is diagonal.
hypothesis: The root cause is an inefficient algorithmic choice in the Weight class constructor. It creates a full n x n matrix (via MatrixUtils.createRealMatrix) to store weights, even though the weights are diagonal. For large n, this leads to an O(n^2) memory allocation that exceeds the heap space.
prediction: The fix will involve changing the Weight class to store the weights in a more memory-efficient structure (e.g., a diagonal matrix representation or a simple vector) instead of a full n x n matrix, avoiding the O(n^2) allocation.
experiment_rationale: The stack trace points directly to the Weight constructor calling MatrixUtils.createRealMatrix(dim, dim), which allocates a full matrix. The bug report confirms that this n x n allocation is the source of the memory exhaustion when n is large.
reasoning_summary: The defect is an algorithmic inefficiency. The procedure for storing weights is fundamentally flawed for large datasets because it uses a dense matrix representation where a sparse (diagonal) representation is sufficient. This is a procedural/computational strategy error rather than a missing guard (Checking), a wrong constant (Assignment), or a design-level capability gap (Function/Class/Object).
evidence_used: Bug report description: 'When using the Weigth class to pass a large number of weights to multivariate vector optimizers, an nxn full matrix is created (and copied) when a n elements vector is used.'

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the fix might involve changing the internal storage of the Weight class, the root cause is the choice of an inefficient algorithm (dense matrix) for a task that can be performed with a more efficient one (diagonal matrix), which is a classic Algorithm/Method defect.
There is no missing guard or validation; the code is performing exactly what it was programmed to do (allocate an n x n matrix), but the algorithm chosen for that task is inefficient.
